title: Hardware Page-Table Walk
summary: What actually happens, step by step, the moment a TLB miss forces the hardware to go find a translation the slow way.

slides.markdown:
A **TLB miss** doesn't stop execution — it triggers a **page-table walk**: a sequence of memory reads, one per page-table level, that follows the mapping down to the physical frame. On architectures with a hardware walker, this whole process happens without ever interrupting the running program.

The walk itself is not free — it touches memory just like any other access, which means it can miss in the *data* cache too, compounding the cost of the original TLB miss.

slides.subTitle: The TLB miss handoff
slides.markdown:
The moment the TLB reports a miss for a given virtual address, the hardware (or OS, on software-managed designs) must locate the correct page-table entry. On hardware-walked architectures, this is handled by dedicated circuitry — the **page-table walker** — with no software involvement at all; the CPU simply stalls the requesting instruction until the walk resolves.

The walker starts from a known root — a register (like x86's CR3) holds the physical address of the top-level page table for the currently running process.

slides.subTitle: Walking through several levels
slides.markdown:
Starting from the top-level table's known address, each level's index selects one entry, pointing to the next level or, at the final level, the physical frame directly.

![A step-by-step walk through multiple page-table levels, one memory read per level, to resolve a single virtual address](assets/hardware-page-walk-steps.svg)

Each arrow is a real memory read — a 4-level walk costs up to 4 extra accesses before the real access even begins.

slides.subTitle: The page-table walker as a state machine
slides.markdown:
The **hardware page-table walker** is a small dedicated state machine — it isn't the general-purpose core running a program; it's fixed logic whose only job is issuing the sequence of memory reads a walk needs, level by level, and feeding the result back into the TLB once resolved.

Because it's dedicated hardware rather than a software routine, the walk never traps into the OS and never disturbs the pipeline's normal instruction stream the way a full exception would — the requesting instruction simply waits, and everything else can, in many designs, keep making progress.

slides.subTitle: Caching intermediate levels
slides.markdown:
Re-walking all four levels from scratch on every miss is wasteful when nearby translations often share upper-level entries — two pages in the same region likely share the same top-level and second-level entries, differing only near the bottom.

Many CPUs cache these intermediate-level entries in small dedicated structures (sometimes called page-walk caches), so a subsequent miss for a *nearby* address can skip the top levels of the walk entirely and jump straight to resolving just the lower levels — cutting a 4-level walk down to one or two actual memory reads.

slides.subTitle: Hardware walker vs software-handled miss
slides.markdown:
| | Hardware walker | Software-handled (trap + OS routine) |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Lower — no trap | Higher — full trap plus handler execution |
| Flexibility | Fixed page-table format the walker understands | OS can use any table format/policy it wants |
| Transparency | Invisible to software | Visible as an exception, handled in OS code |

Hardware walkers (x86-style) trade flexibility for speed — the format the walker understands is fixed at the ISA level. Software-handled misses (classic MIPS-style) cost more per miss (a real trap into OS code) but let the OS define translation structures however it wants.

slides.subTitle: The walk itself isn't free of cache effects
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A TLB miss just costs a fixed, predictable number of extra memory accesses."

**Why it's wrong:** each walk step is an ordinary memory read, and those can themselves miss in the data cache. Under cache pressure, one TLB miss can turn into several *cache* misses too, each far pricier than a hit — so real cost varies with cache state, not a fixed number.

**Correct model:** a TLB miss's true cost is its memory pattern interacting with the rest of the cache hierarchy — worst case is far above best case, which is why page-walk caches matter so much in practice.
